claims.text: The starting nanoparticles contain at least five metals in near-equal atomic ratios and form a random, single-phase solid solution.
Structural and chemical stability from 473 to 1923 K is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and thermally activated atomic mobility.
High configurational entropy promotes sluggish atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy suppresses phase separation.
Increasing temperature activates atomic mobility that can produce chemical short-range order or precipitates.
At lower temperatures, sluggish diffusion kinetically inhibits atomistic rearrangement.
A single-phase high-entropy alloy can remain free of precipitates under low-temperature exposure.
At higher temperatures, atomic mobility can overcome kinetic barriers to ordering and precipitation.
Short-range order changes the transport properties of a random equiatomic quinary high-entropy alloy.
Short-range order or precipitation disrupts compositional uniformity.
Nanoparticles retaining a random solid solution will maintain stable catalytic behavior.
Nanoparticles retaining a random solid solution will maintain stable thermoelectric behavior.
Formation of short-range order will alter or degrade thermoelectric performance relative to the initial random state.
Formation of short-range order or precipitates will degrade catalytic performance.
The temperature and time threshold for ordering or precipitation varies with elemental system and environment.
Identical samples aged at different temperatures and times are to be compared with the initial unaged baseline.
The hypothesis is falsified if detectable short-range order or precipitation occurs without a performance change, or if performance degrades without detectable microstructural change.
